Goldman says hyperscalers can easily earn 15% on AI, but neoclouds face a utilisation trap
body: The views point to a widening gap in how investors treat the AI trade. Hyperscaler stocks and investment-grade bonds look the most defensible, given their strong balance sheets and cash flows outside AI. Neocloud equity and high-yield credit carry the most risk if utilisation disappoints. Goldman's credit team expects the high-yield market for AI deals to split more sharply, with investors favouring top-tier developers and projects backed by solid contracts. Chipmakers and memory suppliers ultimately depend on the same thing as the neoclouds: evidence that companies using AI are earning a return. The next earnings round's commentary on returns on capital is likely to move the whole complex.

Goldman's analysis suggests the tech giants can comfortably earn a return on their AI build-out, but the neoclouds renting out GPU capacity are exposed if corporate customers keep failing to turn AI spending into profit.

Is the artificial intelligence spending boom built to last? Goldman Sachs put that question to two people who see the cycle from very different vantage points, and their answers point the same way. The biggest technology companies are well placed to ride out a slowdown. The risk is concentrated among newer, more heavily indebted players further down the chain.

Goldman's lead US internet analyst, Eric Sheridan, argued in the bank's November Top of Mind report that the six largest US hyperscalers can "very easily" earn a return on invested capital of 15% or more on their AI spending. Their revenue backlogs are much larger than two or three years ago, and some companies have said about half of those backlogs will turn into revenue within two years. On Goldman's estimates, the hyperscalers would not need anywhere near all of that backlog to convert to reach the 15% mark. Sheridan pointed to the latest earnings round, in which several of the big names gave detailed return figures and their shares rallied, as evidence that the payoff is starting to show.

He described the market's current doubts as understandable, rather than either warranted or overblown. Every computing cycle he has covered, from desktop to mobile to cloud, has gone through a phase of disillusionment once spending runs ahead of visible returns. Investors, he said, want returns within months on a build-out that typically plays out over five to eight years.

Chamath Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of Social Capital, invests across AI chips, power and software. He is more worried about the neoclouds, the specialist firms that rent out GPU capacity. He compares them to a bank in reverse: their revenue is short-term and uncertain, while their obligations for chips, power and data centres are long-dated and fixed. Like airlines, they need to keep their capacity busy to make money. He puts the break-even point at roughly 70% to 75% utilisation, with profits only coming above that. Yearly chip upgrades and more efficient AI models make the arithmetic harder.

His central concern is that big companies are not yet earning a meaningful return on their AI spending. Projects are hard to implement, staff are often wary, and productivity gains tend to get lost elsewhere in the business, so few firms can point to AI as a source of earnings growth. If that remains the case, demand for computing power may not grow fast enough to fill the capacity being built.

Goldman's analysts put the hurdle in numbers. For the hyperscalers to earn a 15% return on their 2026 and 2027 investment, they would need to generate around $1.4 trillion in cumulative revenue over 2028 to 2030, roughly $500 billion a year. Sheridan sees three things that could stall the cycle: weaker demand, a disruption in access to capital, or a shortage of power, which cannot be scaled up as fast as land, buildings or chips. For now, he sees demand gaining momentum rather than fading.

Both expect the cycle to produce winners and losers. Palihapitiya expects a bump in the road at some point, much like the internet build-out two decades ago, which ultimately proved right but got the timing wrong. Neoclouds that own their power and land should hold up better than those that simply lease capacity.

Gold's 37% slide from record looks overdone, says Saxo's Hansen, but $3,590 is the test
body: Gold's moves are being set by the dollar and US rate pricing, not by safe-haven demand, so US data and Fed commentary will matter more than geopolitical headlines for any rebound. Because speculative positioning has been cut so hard, short covering could make any bounce sharp, especially in silver, the most stretched metal. A failure back below Wednesday's low would suggest forced selling has further to run. That would be a risk for miners and leveraged exposure. A softer dollar or a dovish shift in Fed expectations is the catalyst most likely to turn a technical rebound into a lasting one.

Gold has gone from historic exuberance to historic distress in less than a year, and while stretched positioning and a strong seasonal record point to a bounce, Saxo's Ole Hansen says a lasting recovery needs the dollar and rate expectations to ease.

Gold's selloff has swung from one historic extreme to another, and Saxo's head of commodity strategy, Ole Hansen, now sees early signs that the selling may be running out of steam. He cautions that any lasting recovery still depends on the macro backdrop turning in the metal's favour.

In January, gold traded about 45% above its 200-day moving average, the widest gap since the 1970s. This week it slipped about 20% below that average, the deepest negative gap since June 2013, Hansen wrote in a note published by Saxo. That compares with roughly 20% below during the 2008 financial crisis and about 27% below in 1981. Gold is down about 19% this year and around 37% from January's record high, its biggest 12-month drawdown since the early 1980s. The rest of the sector has fared worse. Silver has fallen about 43% this year and sits more than 37% below its 200-day average. Platinum is down about 39%, and palladium is around a third below its trend.

Hansen blames a broad move out of risk rather than a collapse in gold's longer-term case. A strong dollar, energy-driven inflation, rising expectations of rate hikes, turmoil in AI-linked stocks and negative momentum have all pushed investors to raise cash. Higher rate expectations also make it more expensive to hold metals that pay no yield. He argues the long-term supports remain in place, including central banks diversifying their reserves, fiscal worries and demand for assets without counterparty risk. But he says these alone are unlikely to stop the selling.

The setup for a rebound is improving. Short-term momentum readings across the sector are at or below oversold levels, and speculative positioning has been cut substantially. Gold ETF holdings have held up relatively well, and silver has drawn fresh ETF demand despite falling prices. Seasonality also helps: gold has gained over December and January in each of the past 11 years. Hansen stresses that neither oversold conditions nor the calendar is a reason to buy on its own.

He sets out clear technical markers. Gold formed a hammer candle at its recent low near $3,430, a pattern that can signal selling exhaustion. A daily close above about $3,590 would confirm a rebound and open the way to around $3,700, a 38.2% retracement of the November selloff. A fresh break below Wednesday's low would cancel that view. For silver, a daily close above roughly $41.50 would be the equivalent confirmation.

Hansen is also less convinced than markets that the Federal Reserve needs to deliver the rate hikes now priced in. He argues that weaker AI investment, falling diesel prices and a negative wealth effect from lower stock prices could cool inflation and change the Fed's course. A rally driven by short covering could come quickly. A durable recovery, though, would need a softer dollar, lower real yields and calmer stock markets, which he says would not require a renewed AI boom.

news.title: NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears
body: Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement.

Cheaper fuel has pushed Kiwi consumer confidence back above 100 and pulled inflation expectations to a 22-month low, but households still feel better about the future than the present and remain wary of big purchases.

New Zealand consumer confidence climbed back above the 100 mark in November. Falling fuel prices pulled households' inflation expectations to their lowest level in nearly two years, and both the current and future measures of sentiment improved.

The ANZ-Roy Morgan Consumer Confidence index rose 4 points to 100.2, its strongest reading since January, according to the survey released on Friday. That is still well short of the long-run average of 112, so the recovery from April's low near 80 is not complete. Both components improved. The future conditions index rose to around 111 from 106, while the current conditions index edged up to around 84 from 81.

The biggest shift came in inflation expectations. Households now see prices rising 3.9% a year over the next two years, down from 4.2% in October and the lowest since January 2025. That is a steep fall from April's 6.6%, when a spike in pump prices pushed expectations sharply higher. The survey's authors noted that consumers' price expectations fell slightly more than fuel prices over the month, after tracking them almost one-for-one earlier in the year. They also pointed out that inflation expectations and confidence have moved in opposite directions in recent years, which suggests the two are linked.

The economic outlook improved but stayed gloomy for the next 12 months. A net 6% of respondents expect bad times for the economy over that period, compared with a net 13% a month earlier. The five-year view rose to a net 16% positive from 8%, close to its long-run average of 19%. Views on household finances were mixed. A net 20% said they were worse off than a year ago, a marginal improvement. A net 22% expect to be better off a year from now, down from 24% but far above April's low of 3%.

Appetite for spending remains soft. A net 12% still think it is a bad time to buy a major household item, although that is a 6-point improvement on October. House price expectations rose to 2.3% from 2.0%, still well below the survey's 3.5% average.

The survey's authors described the overall mood as below par, citing broader cost-of-living pressures and a soft labour market. They cautioned that consumers' inflation expectations carry less weight for monetary policy than those of businesses, which actually set prices. Households feel better about the future than about the present, which suggests they are not yet ready to spend freely. The next survey is due on December 18.

news.title: Tokyo CPI preview: core inflation seen jumping to 3% three weeks before BoJ decision
body: A firm Tokyo print would add support for the yen, which is still trading near 160 per dollar despite close to $100 billion of intervention. The Fed is also hiking, so the rate gap stays wide, and a BoJ hike on its own may not change the yen's direction much without signs of a quicker pace afterwards. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields are the most exposed if the core-core measure meets or beats forecast. A miss would likely weigh on the yen and could revive talk of the BoJ pausing, especially if Nikkei weakness continues.

Tokyo inflation is expected to rise to around 3% on both core gauges today, giving markets their last clean read on price pressure before a Bank of Japan meeting widely tipped to deliver a third hike of 2026.

Main article: Tokyo's November consumer price data, due at 23:30 GMT (18:30 US Eastern) on Thursday, Friday morning in Japan, is expected to show a sharp pickup in inflation in the capital. It arrives three weeks before a Bank of Japan meeting at which a rate hike is widely expected.

Consensus looks for core Tokyo CPI, which strips out fresh food, to jump to 3.0% from 2.6% in October. The measure that excludes both fresh food and energy is also forecast at 3.0%, up from 2.4%. The BoJ watches that measure more closely as a guide to underlying, demand-driven price pressure. Headline Tokyo inflation ran at 2.8% in October. If the forecasts are met, every key gauge would sit well above the central bank's 2% target.

The Tokyo figures matter because they come out roughly three weeks before the nationwide numbers. They are an imperfect guide: spending in the capital differs from the rest of the country, and nationwide core inflation was only around 2.2% in October. Still, the direction usually carries over. The timing gives the Tokyo release extra weight this month. The nationwide November data is not due until 23:30 GMT on December 17 (18:30 US Eastern). That is the morning of December 18 in Tokyo, the second and final day of the BoJ's December 17 to 18 meeting, so the national data will land only hours before the policy announcement and too late to shape much of the debate. Today's numbers are effectively the last major inflation reading markets can absorb before the decision.

Expectations for that meeting are firm. A Reuters poll published last week found 86% of economists expect the BoJ to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.50% from 1.25%. That would make 2026 Japan's first year with three hikes since the late 1980s. Nearly 60% of respondents expect a further rise to 1.75% by the end of March. Market pricing has been a little more cautious, implying odds of a December move of roughly 75% to 80%.

The hawkish case has also gained support from inside the bank. Board member Naoki Tamura said this week that the BoJ should respond quickly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by raising rates faster. In his view, the Middle East war, higher import costs from the weak yen and strong demand for AI-related goods all pose upside risks to prices, and the policy rate is still some way below neutral.

There are risks to a hike. Japan's economy shrank in the July to September quarter, and a sharp slide in the Nikkei this month has raised questions about whether the bank might pause. Most economists in the Reuters poll said stock market volatility would not stop a December hike, though a prolonged selloff remains the main risk to that view.

A reading at or above forecast would strengthen the case for a hike. A soft reading, especially in the measure that excludes fresh food and energy, would give the bank's more cautious members something to point to. Even so, one miss is unlikely to overturn a move that policymakers have been preparing markets for.

news.title: CoreWeave bond yields are approaching 19%. Why even stock investors should pay attention
body: CoreWeave's falling bond prices offer a warning about the financial risks behind that expansion, even as demand for AI computing continues to grow.

Investors following CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) may want to look beyond its stock chart. On November 25, the yield on one of the company's bonds reached 17.91%, while another traded at a record-low price consistent with a yield of approximately 18.6%.
For shareholders, this is a development worth understanding as the stock is not too far from its all time low, apx 9% above its IPO opening price and still over 77% below its all time high
When a company issues a bond, it is essentially borrowing money from investors. In return, it promises to pay interest and repay the principal according to agreed terms.
Let's take CoreWeave's 9.75% bond, due in October 2031, as an example.
Someone purchasing the bond at that price would pay $742.30 for a security scheduled to repay $1,000 at maturity, while also receiving interest payments along the way.
Assuming CoreWeave meets all its payment obligations, the discounted purchase price helps explain the considerably higher annualized yield.
But why would existing investors sell such a bond at a steep discount?
They may be concerned about the company's ability to repay its debt, require greater compensation for taking that risk, or prefer to reduce their exposure altogether.
When bond prices fall, their yields rise. An exceptionally high corporate bond yield is often a warning rather than a bargain.

CoreWeave provides the computing infrastructure that companies use to develop and operate artificial intelligence applications. Building that infrastructure requires expensive chips, data centers, electricity and substantial upfront investment.
Its third-quarter financial results illustrate the financial challenge:
Quarterly revenue: $3.66 billion, up approximately 168% year over year.
Expected 2026 capital expenditure: $37 billion to $39 billion.
